a: dressed like a shepherd
p: The angel who gives the book its name comes dressed as a herdsman, with goatskin, bag and staff.
b: The man is 'glorious to look at' but wears a working shepherd's gear: a white goatskin, a bag (Greek pēra, the bag Jesus told the Twelve not to take, Matthew 10:10) and a staff. From here on he is Hermas's teacher, and he names himself 'the angel of repentance' (25:7). The book is called The Shepherd after him. The picture draws on the Bible's shepherds of God's people (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34; John 10:11), but this shepherd is an angel sent to one man and his household, not the Lord himself.

a: the most revered angel
p: Hermas does not name the angel who sends the Shepherd; later the book calls him 'the glorious angel'.
b: Greek ho semnotatos angelos, 'the most revered (or most holy) angel'. The same title returns in 33:7, where 'all were justified' by him. In the Similitudes the Shepherd says that the glorious angel gave him to Hermas's house to live there (78:3, Similitude 9.1.3), and the glorious angel is angry at the sins of Hermas's household (66:2). Lake's introduction speaks of 'the great angel, who is in charge of Christians'. Whether this great angel is Michael, the Son of God, or an angel the book never names is argued in the chapter pages of the Similitudes (77; 89-90).

a: the one I was handed over to
p: Hermas says he already knows his guardian, though the Visions never said he had one.
b: Greek hō paredothēn, 'to whom I was handed over', said three times in two verses. Hermas speaks as though he had been entrusted to a guardian angel, and the Shepherd says he is that guardian. Lake's note: 'There is no mention of this in the preceding Visions.' Lake calls the section 'clearly intended as an introduction to the Mandates', which would explain a link the Visions never made. On whether each believer has a guardian angel, see the cards at Matthew 18:10 and Psalm 91.

a: his form changed
p: The angel looks at first like a stranger, then shows who he is.
b: Greek ēlloiōthē hē idea autou, 'his form was changed'. The Shepherd changes again in 47:1, when his anger is more than a human can bear. Angels in the Bible also come looking like ordinary men and are recognized only later (Genesis 18:2; Judges 13:16-21; Tobit 5:4-5, where Tobias does not know that Raphael is an angel). Hermas's fear and grief at having spoken rudely follow the pattern of people who meet an angel (Judges 13:22; Luke 1:12).

a: my commandments, the ones I am about to command you
p: The Shepherd names the two books that follow: the commandments (Mandates) and the parables (Similitudes).
b: Greek entolai, 'commandments', and parabolai, 'parables'. The book's later readers called the second part the Similitudes, from the Latin similitudines (Lake's note at 50:0), and the first part the Mandates, from Latin mandata. Lake calls this chapter 'clearly intended as an introduction to the Mandates, but it is always quoted as the Fifth Vision'. The Plain English Translation keeps 'commandment' and 'parable' in the text and uses 'Mandate' and 'Similitude' only in headings and references.

a: read them at any time
p: The Greek says 'under hand': the commandments are to be ready to read whenever they are needed.
b: Greek hypo cheira, literally 'under the hand', that is, close by, always at hand. The same phrase comes back in 31:6, where it means sinning 'again and again', as a habit. Here it describes a book meant for daily use, read over and over, not a vision to be heard once.

a: the angel of repentance
p: The Shepherd's title: the angel God put in charge of repentance.
b: Greek ho angelos tēs metanoias. Hermas's whole book turns on this title. The Shepherd says, 'I am in charge of repentance' (30:2), and 'the authority over this repentance was given to me' (31:5). In the New Testament there is "joy breaks out before God's angels over one sinner who repents" (Luke 15:10), but no angel is put in charge of repentance. Clement of Alexandria quotes Hermas by this title: 'the Shepherd, the angel of repentance', says it 'to Hermas' (Stromata 1.17.85, quoting 43:3).

a: First of all
p: Irenaeus quotes this verse with 'the Scripture declared', a sign that some early readers took Hermas as Scripture.
b: Irenaeus, writing about AD 180, opens a passage on God the Creator with this verse: 'Truly, then, the Scripture declared, which says, First of all believe that there is one God, who has established all things, and completed them' (Against Heresies 4.20.2, in the English of the Ante-Nicene Fathers). His Greek here survives because Eusebius copied it: Irenaeus, he says, 'not only knows, but also receives the writing of the Shepherd' (ou monon oiden, alla kai apodechetai tēn tou Poimenos graphēn), and he quotes the opening words (Church History 5.8.7). The book-level pages give how the other early lists treated the book.

a: believe that God is one
p: The creed of Israel stands at the head of the commandments.
b: Hermas puts first what Israel put first: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). James uses nearly the same Greek words, 'You believe that God is one' (James 2:19), and adds that faith which stops there is not enough. Hermas does not stop there: the next verse goes on to fear, self-control and every virtue. Paul's form of the confession, 'there is one God, the Father ... and there is one Lord, Jesus Christ' (1 Corinthians 8:6), names the Son; Hermas's commandments never use the names Jesus or Christ.

a: out of what did not exist
p: Hermas says plainly that God made everything 'out of what is not into being'.
b: Greek ek tou mē ontos eis to einai, 'out of what is not into being'. Lake's margin points to 2 Maccabees 7:28, where a mother tells her son, 'Know that God made them, not from things that were', and to Wisdom of Solomon 1:14 ('He created everything to exist'). Hebrews 11:3 says the visible world did not come 'out of what appears'. Hermas says it plainly: God made all things from nothing. Irenaeus quoted the verse (see the note on 'First of all').
r: 2 Maccabees 7:28; Wisdom of Solomon 1:14; Hebrews 11:3; Romans 4:17; Ephesians 3:9

a: he alone cannot be held
p: God 'contains' everything, but nothing contains him.
b: Greek panta chōrōn, monos de achōrētos ōn, 'holding (containing) all things, but being alone uncontainable'. The verb chōreō means 'to have room for' or 'to hold', like a jar. The picture fits the book: in 33:2 and 34:5 the human 'vessel' has room for the Holy Spirit or for evil spirits, but not both. God, by contrast, makes room for all things and is held by no place, as Solomon prays: "the heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you" (1 Kings 8:27).

a: you will live to God
p: The refrain of the Mandates: life lived toward God, now and in the life to come.
b: Greek zēsē tō theō, 'you will live to (or for) God'. The phrase closes almost every commandment (27:6; 28:5; 30:4; 32:3; 36:10; 37:4; 38:12; 39:12; 42:4; 46:1; 49:5). In 37:5 the Shepherd explains it: all creation fears God, but only those who also keep his commandments 'have life with God'. Paul uses the same dative: "alive to God" (Romans 6:11), "live for God" (Galatians 2:19). For Hermas it means both a life given to God now and the life he gives at the end.

a: be self-controlled
p: Mandate 1 names three things, and Mandates 6 to 8 come back to explain each.
b: Greek enkrateusai, 'be self-controlled', from enkrateia, 'self-control' (as Galatians 5:23 on the site). The Shepherd later says, 'In the first commandment ... I commanded you to keep faith, fear and self-control' (35:1), and then takes them in turn: faith (Mandate 6, 35-36), fear (Mandate 7, 37) and self-control (Mandate 8, 38). In Mandate 8 the verb is 'hold back from', the same Greek word.

a: Hold on to simplicity
p: Greek haplotēs: a single, undivided heart, the opposite of the 'double-minded'.
b: Greek haplotēs, 'simplicity, singleness', from haplous, 'single, not folded'. It is the virtue of the whole commandment: give 'simply' (27:4, 27:6), serve 'simply' (27:6), and let repentance be found 'in simplicity' (27:7). It is the opposite of the double-minded heart of Mandate 9. Paul uses the word for generous giving (Romans 12:8; 2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:11), and James says God gives haplōs, 'with an open hand' (James 1:5).

a: you will be like little children
p: Innocence like a child's, who does not yet know evil.
b: Jesus said, "if you do not turn around and become like the little children, you will not get into the kingdom of heaven at all" (Matthew 18:3). Hermas's point is narrower and closer to Paul's: "Be little children when it comes to evil, but when it comes to thinking, be fully grown" (1 Corinthians 14:20). The innocent person here is not ignorant of everything, only of 'the wickedness that destroys people's lives'. Children return as a picture of innocence in Similitude 9 (106, the twelfth mountain).

a: do not slander anyone
p: The one who listens with pleasure shares the slanderer's sin.
b: Greek katalaleō, 'speak against, run down'. Lake's margin points to James 4:11, the same verb: "Brothers, stop running one another down". Hermas adds something James does not say: the listener who believes the slander becomes guilty too, because he now holds something against his brother. The site's topic on speech gathers the Bible's warnings on gossip and slander.

a: It is a restless demon
p: Slander is pictured as an evil spirit that never settles down.
b: Greek akatastaton daimonion, 'an unsettled (unstable) demon'. James calls the tongue 'an unsettled evil' with the same adjective (James 3:8), and calls the double-minded man akatastatos (James 1:8). Hermas often speaks of vices as spirits that live in a person (33:3-4; 34:5-7; 39:11). Whether he means real demons or vivid pictures of the passions, the text treats them as forces a person must 'keep away from'.

a: give to all who are in need, simply, without hesitating
p: Lake: the same rule is in the Didache, which calls it 'the commandment'.
b: Lake's note: 'This series of precepts is also found in the Didache (i. 5) and is there quoted as being "according to the commandment"'. The Didache says: "For the Father wants his own gracious gifts to be given to all" (Didache 1:5), close to Hermas's 'God wants his own gifts given to all'. 'Without hesitating' (mē distazōn) recalls the Two Ways: "You must not hesitate to give, and you must not grumble when you give" (Didache 4:7; Epistle of Barnabas 19:11). Whether Hermas used the Didache, the Didache used Hermas, or both drew on a common teaching, cannot be settled from these few words.
r: Didache 1:5; Didache 4:7; Epistle of Barnabas 19:11; Matthew 5:42; Luke 6:30

a: will give an account to God
p: The giver is innocent; the one who takes under false pretenses must answer for it.
b: Hermas moves the burden from the giver to the receiver. The Didache makes the same move: the one who takes without need "will have to pay the penalty: why did he take it, and for what?" (Didache 1:5). Hermas uses the same two questions, 'why ... and for what'. In a city church that supported widows, orphans and the poor, the question of who deserved help was real (2 Thessalonians 3:10; 1 Timothy 5:3-16). Hermas's answer is to give freely and leave the judging to God.

a: a task of service
p: Greek diakonia: the giver carries out a service God gave him.
b: Greek diakonia, 'service, ministry', the word behind 'deacon'. The giver has 'received from the Lord' the task of giving and 'carried it out simply'. Paul calls the collection for Jerusalem 'this service' (2 Corinthians 9:12-13), with the same word. In 46:3 the Shepherd gives Hermas another diakonia: to urge everyone to repent.

a: the spirit God made to live in this flesh
p: A human spirit God gave, or the Holy Spirit living in the believer? Hermas's Greek allows both.
b: Greek to pneuma ho ho theos katōkisen en tē sarki tautē, 'the spirit which God made to dwell in this flesh'. In 28:2 the liar hands back 'a spirit that does not lie' as a liar; in 28:4 Hermas has grieved 'the spirit that is reverent and true'. The Holy Spirit may be meant, because 'grief' brought on the spirit echoes Ephesians 4:30, and because in 33:2 and 41:6 Hermas speaks of the Holy Spirit living in the believer's flesh. Or Hermas may mean the human spirit God breathed into each person (Genesis 2:7; Ecclesiastes 12:7). The Plain English Translation writes 'spirit' with a small letter here, as the Greek does not decide; in 33-34 and 40-42, where Hermas says 'the Holy Spirit', it uses the capital.

a: the deposit they received
t: A deposit to be handed back
p: The spirit is a trust held for its owner, to be returned as it was given.
b: Greek parakatathēkē, a legal word for property left in someone's keeping, which must be returned whole. Lake's margin points to 2 Timothy 1:14: "Keep the good deposit safe through the Holy Spirit, who has made his home in us." The liar who returns the spirit 'as a liar' is like a trustee who embezzles. So Hermas calls liars 'people who rob the Lord' (Greek apostērētai, 'defrauders').

a: Because, sir
p: Hermas calls the Shepherd kyrie, the same word the book uses for 'the Lord'.
b: Greek kyrie. When Hermas speaks to the Shepherd, the Plain English Translation writes 'sir', because Hermas is addressing an angel, his teacher. When the book speaks of ho kyrios, God or Christ, it writes 'the Lord'. Greek has one word for both, so a reader of the Greek hears the respect in Hermas's address and the faith in his worship with the same sound. Mary Magdalene uses the word for the man she takes to be a gardener (John 20:15).

a: I have always spoken craftily with everyone
p: Hermas admits a life of clever half-truths in business, and no one ever caught him.
b: Greek panourgōs, 'craftily, with all-round cleverness'. Hermas, a former slave (1:1), seems to have been a man of business: the Shepherd speaks of 'the lies you told before in your business dealings' (28:5), and the book often warns about business and wealth (40:4; 14:5). His tears are the turning point of the commandment.

a: brought grief on the spirit that is reverent and true
p: Hermas's words echo Paul's warning not to grieve the Holy Spirit.
b: Paul: "And do not cause grief to the Holy Spirit of God. In him you were sealed, for the day of redemption" (Ephesians 4:30). Hermas uses the same noun, lypē, 'grief'. Mandate 10 (40-42) builds a whole teaching on it: grief 'wears out the Holy Spirit' (40:2), and Lake's margin there also points to Ephesians 4:30. Isaiah 63:10 says Israel "grieved his holy spirit".

a: I have never understood words like these so clearly
p: The Greek says 'heard', but Lake notes the sense is 'understood'.
b: Greek akribōs ēkousa, 'I heard accurately'. Lake's note: 'The literal meaning of the Greek is "heard," but the meaning is clearly much more nearly "understood."' The Plain English Translation follows the sense. The Shepherd's answer plays on the verb: 'Well, now you are hearing them' (28:5).

a: may become believable
p: Lake: Hermas must act so that what he promised falsely becomes true in fact.
b: The sentence is hard. Lake's note: 'The meaning is obscure, but it appears to be that Hermas having made untrue statements in the course of business must try so to act that his statements will be justified in fact; for instance, if he had made extravagant promises he must fulfil them.' Another reading takes it more simply: once Hermas is known as a truthful man, people will trust him again, and even his old words will be believed. Either way, repentance here has a practical side, like Zacchaeus's paying back four times over (Luke 19:8).

a: keep yourself pure
p: Greek hagneia: sexual purity, which for Hermas begins in the thoughts.
b: Greek hagneia, 'purity, chastity'. Hermas begins where Jesus began: not only the deed but the thought that 'comes into the heart' about another man's wife (Matthew 5:28). Vision 1 started with exactly such a thought, about Rhoda (1:2-8), so the commandment answers Hermas's own first sin. The word returns in 31:2 ('make his home in purity') and 32:3-4.

a: he brings about his own death
p: The thought is a great sin; the deed brings death.
b: James traces the same steps: desire "gives birth to sin, and sin, once it is grown, bears death" (James 1:15; compare Romans 6:23). Hermas distinguishes the thought, 'a great sin for a slave of God', from the deed, which 'works death'. The phrase 'slave of God' (doulos theou) is one of Hermas's names for every believer.

a: He must divorce her
p: The husband must send away a wife who will not repent, but may not marry again, so she can come back.
b: Greek apolysatō, 'let him send (her) away', the word the Gospels use for divorce. Lake's note: 'This mandate is really explaining the practical problem which arose from the conflict between the Christian precept against divorce (Mk. 10, 11 f.) and the equally early precept against having intercourse with immoral persons.' Jesus says, "anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual sin, and marries someone else commits adultery" (Matthew 19:9); Paul tells a wife who separates that "she is to stay single, or else be reconciled with her husband" (1 Corinthians 7:11). Lake adds that Hermas's separation 'was not strictly divorce, as the innocent party was not free to remarry in order to give the other the opportunity of repenting and of returning.' How the churches read Jesus' words on divorce and remarriage is set out on the cards at Matthew 5 and 19 and 1 Corinthians 7.

a: For God's slaves there is one repentance
p: The first statement of the book's rule: a single repentance after baptism.
b: Greek tois gar doulois tou theou metanoia estin mia. This is why the husband must take back a repentant wife 'but not over and over'. The rule is explained in 31:1-6, where the Shepherd says that a believer who falls after 'that great and solemn calling' has 'one repentance'. See the chapter page of 31 for how this was read in the early church and later.

a: Whoever does things like the Gentiles do also commits adultery
p: Adultery is not only a sin of the body: living like the pagans is unfaithfulness too.
b: Greek ta homoiōmata poiē tois ethnesin, 'does the likenesses (the same things) as the Gentiles'. The prophets called Israel's idolatry adultery (Hosea 1:2; Jeremiah 3:8-9; Ezekiel 16), and James calls friends of the world "You adulteresses!" (James 4:4). Hermas applies the marriage rule of 29:4-8 to this wider unfaithfulness: if a spouse persists in pagan ways and will not repent, the believer must separate.

a: repentance is possible
p: Staying single keeps the way back open for the one who sinned.
b: The command to 'stay by yourselves' is not punishment of the innocent spouse. It keeps the marriage open, so that the sinner can repent and return. Paul gives a similar reason for a separated wife: 'or else be reconciled with her husband' (1 Corinthians 7:11). The rule holds 'for wife and husband alike' (29:8): the same duty binds both.

a: I am not giving an excuse
p: Hermas guards against the charge that he makes sin easy; Tertullian later made that very charge.
b: Lake's note: 'Hermas is guarding against the imputation that he is lowering the standard of morality. This accusation was actually brought against him later by Tertullian.' Tertullian, after he joined the Montanists, called it 'the scripture of the Shepherd, which alone loves adulterers' (scriptura Pastoris, quae sola moechos amat, On Modesty 10.12) and 'that apocryphal Shepherd of adulterers' (illo apocrypho Pastore moechorum, 20.2). See the chapter page of 31.

a: my heart has been hardened
p: Hermas uses the Gospel word for hearts that cannot understand.
b: Greek pepōrōtai, 'has been hardened, made dull'. Lake's margin points to Mark 6:52, where the disciples "had not grasped what the loaves meant. Instead, their hearts had turned hard." Hermas joins hardness to his past deeds: habits of sin dull the power to understand. The cure the Shepherd offers is repentance, which he calls understanding (30:2).

a: repenting is itself understanding
p: Greek metanoia means a change of mind, and Hermas plays on it: to repent is to understand.
b: Greek metanoia, 'repentance', is built from 'after' and 'mind', and Hermas makes it the same as synesis, 'understanding, insight'. The sinner 'understands' (synīei) what he has done. Clement of Alexandria repeats the point from 'the same' Shepherd: tēn metanoian synesin einai phēsi megalēn, 'he says that repentance is great understanding' (Stromata 2.12-13). 'Done evil before the Lord' echoes the verdict of Judges (Judges 2:11), as Lake's margin notes.

a: He humbles his own soul and punishes it
p: Hermas's repentance includes humbling and 'tormenting' one's own soul.
b: Greek tapeinoi tēn heautou psychēn kai basanizei, 'humbles his own soul and tortures it'. Israel was told to 'humble yourselves' on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Lake saw in Hermas 'the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance', in which repentance includes acts that express sorrow. Read another way, the stress falls on the turning of life: the repentant man 'no longer does evil, but does good'. The verse does not say that the self-humbling earns forgiveness.

a: some teachers
p: Teachers in Rome said there was no repentance after baptism. Lake: possibly Hebrews 6.
b: Lake's note on 'some teachers': 'Possibly a reference to Heb. 6, 4 ff.' Hebrews says it is "impossible to make them new again and bring them to repentance" those who have fallen away (Hebrews 6:6), and that for one who keeps sinning by choice "there is no longer any sacrifice for sins left" (Hebrews 10:26). The teachers may have read Hebrews strictly, or they may simply have taught that baptism was the one fresh start, whatever text they used. The Shepherd agrees with them in principle (31:2) before announcing an exception (31:4-6).

a: went down into the water
p: Hermas's words for baptism: going down into water and receiving forgiveness.
b: Greek eis hydōr katebēmen, 'we went down into water'. Hermas speaks of baptism as the one moment when 'earlier sins' were forgiven (31:3), as Peter said: "Repent, and let each one of you be baptized ... for the forgiveness of your sins" (Acts 2:38). Acts 8:38 says Philip and the official 'went down into the water'. In Similitude 9 Hermas calls baptism 'the seal', by which believers go down into the water dead and come up alive (93-94).

a: for those who were called before these days
p: The second repentance is for those baptized before now, not for future converts.
b: This is the heart of the Shepherd's ruling. New believers have the forgiveness of baptism and need nothing else (31:3). For those already baptized who have since sinned, the Lord 'has set a repentance'. Vision 2 put the same idea as a fixed day: once it has been set, sin will bring no salvation, because repentance for the righteous comes to an end (6:5, Vision 2.2.5). It can be read as a one-time offer to the Roman church of Hermas's day, not a permanent system, or as an early step toward the church's regular practice of reconciling sinners, which is how Lake read it ('the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance').

a: how many-sided the devil's schemes are
p: Greek polyplokia: the devil's 'many-twistedness', his knotted schemes.
b: Greek polyplokia, from 'many' and 'plait, twist'. The Lord gives a second repentance because he knows both human weakness and the devil's skill. The idea of the devil's 'schemes' is Paul's (Ephesians 6:11; 2 Corinthians 2:11); Hermas's word is more vivid.

a: the authority over this repentance was given to me
p: The Shepherd holds authority over repentance. Who on earth holds it is a later question.
b: Greek hē exousia tēs metanoias tautēs. In the Gospels Jesus gives authority to forgive and to bind and loose to his disciples (Matthew 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23). Hermas speaks only of an angel's authority and of Hermas's task to preach this repentance (46:2-3). Hermas never says who in the church declares a sinner restored. Later writers debated whether bishops held this power; the site's cards at Matthew 18 and John 20 give the churches' answers.

a: But I tell you
p: The fourth-century Sinaiticus breaks off here; from now on one late manuscript carries the Greek.
b: Lake's footnote: 'With the φη of φησί the extant leaves of ℵ come to an end.' Codex Sinaiticus, written in the 300s, contains Hermas from 1:1 to the first letters of 'he said' in this verse (Lake's introduction: 'Vis. I. i. 1. to Mandate IV. iii. 6'). From here on the only continuous Greek is the Athos manuscript (A), copied in the 1400s, and transcribed by the forger Simonides; Lake calls both Simonides's copy and Georgandas's collation 'very inaccurate'. Lake checks A against the Latin and Ethiopic versions and the quotations, as in the next sentence.

a: after that great and solemn calling
p: The 'calling' is baptism, the moment the believer was called into the church.
b: Greek meta tēn klēsin ekeinēn tēn megalēn kai semnēn, 'after that great and holy calling'. In context the calling is the moment of baptism in 31:1-3. The adjective semnos ('revered, solemn') is the word of the 'most revered angel' (25:2). Paul speaks of "God's call upward in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 3:14) and asks believers to "walk in a way that fits the calling you received" (Ephesians 4:1).

a: he has one repentance
p: Hermas's rule: one repentance for serious sin after baptism, no more.
b: Hermas does not say how serious a sin must be, but his examples are adultery (29) and, in Vision 2, Hermas's children who rejected God and betrayed their parents (6:2). After the second repentance, the one who 'sins again and again and repents' gains nothing. Catholic practice no longer keeps this limit: the Catechism says the private penance that spread from the seventh century 'envisioned the possibility of repetition' (Catechism 1447). How the churches differ on a believer who falls, and on confession, is on the site's cards at Hebrews 6 ('Can someone who has truly believed fall away?') and Psalm 32 ('Must sins be confessed to a priest?'). The chapter page gives how the early church read this verse.

a: sins again and again
p: The same phrase as 25:5: sin that has become a habit, always at hand.
b: Greek hypo cheira hamartanē, literally 'sins under the hand'. In 25:5 the phrase meant reading the commandments 'at any time'. Here it means sinning as a matter of course, again and again. The Shepherd's warning is aimed at someone who treats repentance as routine, not at someone who stumbles once more.

a: I have come to life again
p: Hermas: hearing this has given him life back.
b: Greek ezōopoiēthēn, 'I was made alive', the verb Paul uses for God's raising the dead (Romans 4:17; Ephesians 2:5 in a compound form). For Hermas, who had feared he could not be saved (28:3), the news of a second repentance is like a return from death. The Shepherd's answer widens the promise to 'all who do these things'.

a: if a wife, or a husband, dies, and the one left behind marries
p: Hermas follows Paul: remarriage after a death is no sin, staying single is better.
b: Greek koimēthē, 'falls asleep', the gentle Christian word for death. Lake's margin points to 1 Corinthians 7:38-40: "But if the husband dies, she is free to marry the man she chooses, but only in the Lord. In my judgment she is more blessed if she stays as she is" (1 Corinthians 7:39-40). Hermas's 'more honor and great glory with the Lord' (32:2) restates Paul's 'more blessed'. The cards at 1 Timothy 3 and Judith 16 ask how the churches weigh remarriage and lifelong widowhood.

a: I will live in your house
p: The angel promises to live in Hermas's household, as he was sent to do.
b: This picks up 25:2 ('sent ... to live with you'). The book often thinks of households: Hermas's own family and their sins (2-3; 66), and the commandments for 'you and your household' (27:7; 33:7). For a church that met in homes in Rome (Romans 16:5), a household was the place where faith was lived.

a: Be patient
p: Greek makrothymia: 'long-temper', the slow-to-anger patience the Bible gives to God.
b: Greek makrothymos, 'patient', literally 'long-tempered'. Its opposite in this commandment is oxycholia, 'quick bile', a sharp, short temper. God himself is 'slow to anger' (Exodus 34:6), and patience is part of the Spirit's fruit (Galatians 5:22). The pairing of patience and understanding (synetos) recalls Proverbs 14:29, where patience goes with great understanding.

a: the Holy Spirit who lives in you will be pure
p: The Holy Spirit lives in the believer like a guest who needs room and peace.
b: Hermas pictures the person as a 'vessel' or house where the Holy Spirit lives (33:2; 34:5). If bad temper moves in, the Spirit is 'choked' and 'tries to leave'. Paul too says the Spirit 'lives in you' (1 Corinthians 3:16) and warns against grieving him (Ephesians 4:30). Hermas goes further than Paul in picturing the Spirit as able to leave a believer. Whether Hermas thinks of the Spirit as a person or as a holy power is one of the questions the book raises. Mandate 10 (40-42) develops the picture.

a: together with the vessel he lives in
p: The 'vessel' is the human person, in which spirits live.
b: Greek skeuos, 'vessel, jar'. Paul speaks of 'clay pots' that hold a treasure (2 Corinthians 4:7) and tells each believer to control 'his own vessel' (1 Thessalonians 4:4). Hermas uses the picture again and again: honey spoiled in a jar (33:5), a vessel that overflows (34:5), an empty jar among full ones (43:13-15), wine jars that go sour (48:3).

a: who is delicate
p: Greek tryphēros: soft, delicate, used for the Spirit and the good angel.
b: Greek tryphēron on, 'being delicate (tender, refined)'. The same adjective describes the Holy Spirit in 34:6 and the angel of righteousness in 36:3. It is related to tryphē, 'luxury', which Hermas condemns (36:5; 45:1), but here it means sensitive and easily driven away, not soft living.

a: wormwood
p: A tiny bit of bitter wormwood spoils a whole jar of honey.
b: Wormwood is a bitter plant. In the Bible it stands for bitterness and judgment (Deuteronomy 29:18; Lamentations 3:19; Revelation 8:11). Hermas makes it a household lesson: no one keeps honey that tastes of wormwood. So with patience: a little temper spoils it, and even its prayer is spoiled (33:6).

a: all of them were justified by the most revered angel
p: A puzzling line: the repentant are 'justified' by the most revered angel.
b: Greek edikaiōthēsan, 'were justified, declared righteous', the word Paul uses for God's verdict on believers (Romans 3:24; 5:1). Hermas gives it to 'the most revered angel' who sent the Shepherd (25:2). If the angel is the Son of God under an angel's title, the line agrees with the New Testament; if he is a created angel, Hermas means at most that this angel approved the penitents. Hermas never explains, and the line is one reason the book's Christology is debated (see the chapter pages of 59 and 89).

a: the empty and double-minded
p: Greek dipsychos: 'two-souled', a word Hermas shares with James.
b: Greek dipsychos, literally 'two-souled'. James uses it: "He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:8). Hermas uses the word and its family again and again, and Mandate 9 (39) is given to it. Here it is paired with 'empty' (apokenos), the picture of 43:13-15 and 48:3-4.

a: from bitterness rage, from rage anger, and from anger lasting fury
p: Five words for anger, each giving birth to the next.
b: Hermas makes a chain: folly gives birth to bitterness (pikria), bitterness to rage (thymos), rage to anger (orgē), anger to lasting fury (mēnis, the grudging wrath of Achilles at the start of the Iliad). Paul lists three of the same words together: "Let all bitterness, rage and anger ... be lifted away from you" (Ephesians 4:31). James 1:15 traces a similar chain for desire.
orig: πικρία, θυμός, ὀργή, μῆνις (pikria, thymos, orgē, mēnis)

a: that vessel cannot hold them all
p: The Holy Spirit and evil spirits cannot share one home: the vessel overflows.
b: The picture explains 33:4: when good and evil spirits 'live in the same place', the person cannot hold them, and the Holy Spirit leaves (34:6). Jesus' saying about the evil spirit that returns to an empty house with "seven more spirits, worse than itself" (Matthew 12:45) lies close to 34:7, where the empty person is filled with evil spirits. Compare 'No one can be a slave to two masters' (Matthew 6:24).

a: their workings go two ways
p: Hermas gives his own form of the Two Ways teaching: a straight road and a crooked one.
b: Greek diplai gar eisin hai energeiai autōn, 'for their workings are double'. The roads of 35:2-4 are the old picture of the two ways: "There are two ways, one of life and one of death" (Didache 1:1); the Epistle of Barnabas sets angels over them (Epistle of Barnabas 18:1), as Hermas does in 36. Jesus spoke of the narrow and the wide road (Matthew 7:13-14), and the Psalms and Proverbs of the straight and crooked path (Psalm 1:6; Proverbs 2:13-15).
r: Didache 1:1; Epistle of Barnabas 18:1; Matthew 7:13-14; Psalm 1:6; Proverbs 2:13-15; Jeremiah 21:8

a: anyone who turns to the Lord with his whole heart
p: The prophets' call to return to the Lord with the whole heart.
b: Lake's margin points to Jeremiah 24:7 and Joel 2:12, where the people 'turn back' to the LORD 'with all your heart'. Hermas repeats the phrase in 39:2, 48:2 and 49:1-2: the whole heart is the cure for the divided heart of the double-minded.

a: Two angels are with each human being
p: Each person has a good angel and a wicked angel, whose 'works' rise up in the heart.
b: Hermas says each human being has two angels, 'of righteousness' and 'of wickedness', and their works are known by what 'comes into your heart'. The nearest text on the site is the Two Ways of Barnabas, with 'light-bringing angels of God' over one way and 'angels of Satan' over the other (Epistle of Barnabas 18:1). Jesus speaks of the 'angels' of the little ones (Matthew 18:10); Hermas adds an evil angel beside the good one. The cards at Matthew 18:10, Psalm 91 and Tobit 5 give how the churches answer whether everyone has a guardian angel.
r: Epistle of Barnabas 18:1; Matthew 18:10; Psalm 91:11; Acts 12:15; Ephesians 6:12

a: The angel of righteousness is delicate and modest, gentle and quiet
p: The good angel is known by the virtues he talks about in the heart.
b: The test is Jesus' test for prophets: "You will know who they are from their fruit" (Matthew 7:16), to which Lake's margin points at 36:4. The good angel's virtues are close to the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23), and the bad angel's works in 36:5 to the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:19-21).

a: desires for women, and grabbing for more
p: Greek pleonexia: wanting more than one's share.
b: Greek pleonexiai, 'greedinesses', the wish always to have more. Paul names it among the sins of the Gentiles (Romans 1:29) and calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5). Hermas's list moves from business and food to drink, luxury, sex, greed and pride: the vices of a well-off city household.

a: is bound to commit some sin
p: Does the evil angel force a faithful person to sin? Hermas speaks strongly, but calls for a choice.
b: Greek dei ... exhamartēsai ti, 'it is necessary that he sin something', and in 36:8 ex anankēs, 'of necessity', the wicked man does some good. Read alone, this sounds as if the angels decide. But the whole commandment calls the reader to choose: 'trust him', 'stand clear of him' (36:3, 36:6). So 'bound' is best taken as 'sure to', if the person lets the angel's thought stay in the heart. Hermas's point is that anyone can fall and anyone can do good, so no one may trust himself or despair of another.

a: to say goodbye to the angel of wickedness
p: Greek apotassomai: to take leave of, renounce.
b: Greek apotaxasthai, 'to say goodbye to, take leave of', the word of Luke 14:33, where a disciple must 'say goodbye to all his possessions'. Here it is a choice made again and again in the heart.

a: Fear the Lord
t: Fear God and keep his commands
p: Hermas's command matches the last words of Ecclesiastes.
b: Lake's margin points to Ecclesiastes 12:13: "Fear God and keep his commands, because this is the whole of being human." Hermas says 'the Lord' where the Greek of Ecclesiastes says 'God'. 'Fear' here is not terror but reverence that leads to obedience, and 37:4 says it works both ways: it keeps a person from evil and moves him to good.

a: do not fear the devil
p: Fear goes with power, and the devil has none over those who fear the Lord.
b: Hermas argues from a rule of everyday life: people fear whoever has power. The devil has none against God's slaves (47:6; 48:2), so he is not to be feared, though his works are (37:3). James says the same: "Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you" (James 4:7). Jesus taught his followers to fear God rather than those who can only kill the body (Matthew 10:28).

a: Self-control goes two ways too
p: The verb of self-control means 'hold back from': from evil, yes; from good, never.
b: Greek enkrateuomai, 'to exercise self-control, to hold oneself back'. The Plain English Translation writes 'hold back from' so the play of the commandment shows: hold back from evil, but do not 'hold back' from good. Some early Christian groups made self-control mean giving up marriage, wine or meat (1 Timothy 4:3); Hermas makes it a matter of evil and good, not of foods or marriage.

a: from holding grudges, and from all abuse
p: Greek mnēsikakia: remembering wrongs, keeping score.
b: Greek mnēsikakia, 'remembering evil', keeping a grudge. It returns in 38:10 ('not holding grudges') and in 39:3, where God himself 'holds no grudge' (amnēsikakos). Blasphēmia here is abuse or insult, not only speech against God, as in Ephesians 4:31.

a: serving widows, looking after orphans
p: A list of the church's care: widows, orphans, slaves, guests, the weak and the fallen.
b: James: "to visit orphans and widows in their trouble" (James 1:27), with the same verb 'visit, look after' (episkeptesthai). Hermas's list shows a Roman church at work: serving widows, ransoming God's slaves, welcoming travelers, respecting the old, encouraging the weak, bringing back those who have stumbled, warning sinners, and not squeezing debtors. Compare Matthew 25:35-36 and Romans 12:13.

a: buying God's slaves out of their troubles
p: Greek lytroō: to ransom, buy free, used of prisoners and slaves.
b: Greek ex anankōn lytrousthai tous doulous tou theou, 'to ransom God's slaves out of necessities'. In Rome this could mean paying debts, buying a believer out of slavery or prison, or bailing out the arrested. 1 Clement, written from Rome, says: "We know of many among us who have handed themselves over into chains so that they could ransom others" (1 Clement 55:2). Hermas himself had been sold as a slave (1:1).

a: for in hospitality, now and then, good is done
p: Lake prints the clause in brackets: in hospitality good is sometimes done.
b: Greek en gar tē philoxenia heurisketai agathopoiēsis pote, 'for in hospitality doing good is found sometimes'. The 'sometimes' (pote) is odd. It may mean that hospitality gives occasions for doing good, now and then; others read pote as 'at some time', and compare those who "have had angels as guests without knowing it" (Hebrews 13:2).

a: Remove double-mindedness from yourself
p: Mandate 9 reads like a sermon on James 1:5-8: ask without doubting.
b: James says: "let him ask in faith and not waver at all" (James 1:6), and "He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:8), to which Lake's margin points at 39:6. Hermas shares James's word dipsychos, 'double-minded', and James's thought that God gives freely and without grudging (James 1:5), as in 39:3; for the doubt itself he uses distazō, 'hesitate'. Whether Hermas knew the letter of James or both drew on a shared way of teaching cannot be decided from the words alone. Hermas's twist is pastoral: the double-mindedness he fights is a sinner's doubt that God will hear him at all (39:1).

a: He holds no grudge
p: Greek amnēsikakos: God 'does not remember evil'.
b: Greek amnēsikakos, 'not remembering evil'. God's forgiveness is described as forgetting: "their sin I will remember no more" (Jeremiah 31:34; compare Hebrews 8:12). The point answers Hermas's fear in 39:1: a sinner may ask, because God is not like people who keep score (38:3).

a: you are receiving what you asked for slowly
p: A delay is not a 'no': it may come from a testing or a sin one does not know.
b: Hermas gives two reasons for slow answers: some testing (peirasmos) or some wrong 'you do not know about'. His cure is to keep asking (39:8), as in Jesus' parables of the friend at midnight and the widow and the judge (Luke 11:5-8; 18:1-8). Blame, if any, belongs to the one who gives up, 'not the One who gives' (39:8; James 1:13).

a: double-mindedness is an earthly spirit from the devil
p: Faith comes 'from above', doubt is 'earthly'.
b: James contrasts the wisdom 'from above' with another: "It belongs to the earth, to the merely natural self, to demons" (James 3:15). Hermas makes the same contrast for faith and double-mindedness, and again for the true and false spirit of prophecy (43:5-6, 43:21), where Lake's margin points to James 3:15.

a: wears out the Holy Spirit, and then again it saves
t: Grief that kills and grief that saves
p: Like Paul, Hermas knows a grief that ruins and a grief that leads to repentance.
b: Paul: "For grief in God's way produces repentance, and it leads to a salvation no one regrets. But the grief of the world produces death" (2 Corinthians 7:10). Hermas explains the two in 41:2-4: grief after failure 'wears out' the Spirit, while grief after a sin, if it brings repentance, 'seems to bring salvation'. But he still tells Hermas to put away grief and put on cheerfulness (41:5; 42:1). The card at 2 Corinthians 7 asks what 'godly grief' is.

a: wears out
p: Greek ektribō: to rub away, wear down, destroy.
b: Greek ektribei, 'rubs out, wears away'. In 41:5 Hermas uses another verb, thlibe, 'press, crush', and in 41:2 'grieves'. Together they picture the Spirit as squeezed out of a person by grief.

a: friendships with Gentiles
p: Believers busy with trade, money and pagan friendships lose the power to understand.
b: Greek philiais ethnikais, 'Gentile friendships'. In Rome, business meant networks of patrons, partners and friends, with meals and rites in honor of the gods. Hermas does not forbid business, but says those 'tangled up' in it cannot understand 'the parables about the divine'. Vision 3 says the same of the rich, who deny the Lord in trouble because of their business (14:5).

a: Good vineyards, when they are neglected
p: A good vineyard left alone goes wild with thorns, and so does a believer's mind.
b: Greek chersountai, 'become barren, go to waste'. Proverbs pictures the sluggard's vineyard overgrown with thorns (Proverbs 24:30-31), Isaiah God's vineyard that grows wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1-6), and Jesus seed choked by thorns, which are "the worries of the age and the trickery of wealth" (Matthew 13:22). Hermas returns to vines and vineyards in Similitudes 2 and 5 (51; 55).

a: they have the fear of the Lord in them
p: Where the Lord lives, there is understanding.
b: Lake's margin points to Psalm 111:10 and Proverbs 1:7, "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7), and to Sirach 2:3, "Hold tight to him and do not turn away". Hermas's 'hold fast to the Lord' uses the same Greek verb as Sirach 2:3, kollēthēti.

a: do not crush the Holy Spirit who lives in you
p: Another echo of 'do not grieve' and 'do not snuff out the Spirit'.
b: Greek mē thlibe, 'do not press, do not crush'. Lake's margin at 41:4 points to Ephesians 4:30 ("do not cause grief to the Holy Spirit of God"). Paul also writes, 'Do not snuff out the Spirit' (1 Thessalonians 5:19). Hermas's fear that the Spirit may 'leave you' is sharper than anything Paul says (see 33:2).

a: the Spirit of God who was given to this flesh
p: God gave his Spirit to live in the human body.
b: Greek to pneuma tou theou to dothen eis tēn sarka tautēn, 'the Spirit of God that was given into this flesh'. The thought is Paul's: "God's Spirit lives in you" (Romans 8:9), and "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (1 Corinthians 6:19). In Similitude 5 Hermas uses similar words for the Spirit living in 'the flesh' of the Son (59:5-7), which part of the book's debate on its Christology turns on.

a: put on cheerfulness
p: Greek hilarotēs: gladness that shows, the opposite of grief.
b: Greek hilarotēs, 'cheerfulness'. Paul says "God loves a glad giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7), with the same Greek word, hilaron. For Hermas cheerfulness is not a mood but a garment one puts on, and the Holy Spirit himself was 'given to people cheerful' (42:2). Joy as a mark of the Spirit runs through the New Testament (Galatians 5:22; Philippians 4:4).

a: by not praying to the Lord or confessing to him
p: Greek exomologeomai can mean confess sins or give praise.
b: Greek mē entynchanōn mēde exomologoumenos tō kyriō. The verb exomologeomai means 'confess' (sins, Matthew 3:6; James 5:16) and also 'acknowledge, give praise' (Matthew 11:25; Romans 15:9). With 'praying' beside it, either sense fits: the grieving man neither asks God for anything nor openly confesses or praises him. The Plain English Translation writes 'confessing'.

a: God's altar
p: Prayers go up to God's altar in heaven; grief weighs them down.
b: Greek thysiastērion, 'altar'. Revelation pictures the prayers of the saints rising with incense from the golden altar before God's throne (Revelation 8:3-4; compare Psalm 141:2). Hermas uses the picture to say that a prayer mixed with grief cannot rise 'pure'.

a: sitting on a bench, and another man sitting on a chair
p: Lake: the bench of the learners, the chair of the teacher.
b: Greek sympsellion, 'bench', and kathedra, 'chair'. Lake's note: 'sympsellion cannot be here translated by the same word as in Vis. III. i. 4. Here it is the "bench" of the learner as opposed to the "chair" of the teacher.' The false prophet sits in the teacher's chair, like the scribes and Pharisees who 'have sat down' on 'Moses' seat' (Matthew 23:2), and the double-minded sit before him to listen.

a: as to a fortune-teller
t: Asking the prophet about the future
p: The double-minded treat the false prophet like a pagan oracle.
b: Greek hōs epi mantin, 'as to a seer, a diviner'. Romans of every class consulted oracles, astrologers and diviners about business, marriage and health. Acts tells of a slave girl whose 'fortune-telling earned a lot of money for her masters' (Acts 16:16), with the related verb. Hermas calls asking a false prophet about the future idol worship (43:4): it treats God's Spirit like a paid oracle.

a: But he also says some true things
p: Clement of Alexandria quotes this verse, naming 'the Shepherd, the angel of repentance'.
b: Clement of Alexandria, writing around AD 200, quotes this sentence almost word for word: 'And the Shepherd, the angel of repentance, also says to Hermas about the false prophet: For he also speaks some true words, for the devil fills him with his own spirit, to see if he can break any of the righteous' (Stromata 1.17.85, in fresh English from the Greek). Clement uses it to explain how false prophets can say true things.

a: are always repenting
p: Repenting often, without real change, is a mark of the double-minded.
b: Greek pyknōs metanoousi, 'they repent often'. This is the same danger as 31:6, the person who 'sins again and again and repents'. Such people go to the fortune-teller because they are never settled. Their 'repentance' is a passing mood, not a turning of life.

a: no spirit given by God has to be questioned
t: The Spirit is not for hire
p: A true prophet does not answer questions on demand: the Spirit speaks when God wills.
b: For Hermas the mark of a false prophet is that he speaks when asked, like an oracle, and is silent unless asked (43:6). The true prophet speaks only when God wants him to (43:8). Peter says, "For no prophecy was ever borne in by human will" (2 Peter 1:21). Prophets of the Hebrew Bible were sometimes asked for a word from the LORD (1 Kings 22:5-8; Jeremiah 21:2), so Hermas's rule fits his own church's problem more than every case in the Bible.

a: a gathering of righteous men
p: Greek synagōgē: the word for a synagogue, used of the Christian assembly.
b: Greek synagōgē, 'gathering', the word behind 'synagogue'. James uses it for a Christian assembly: "Say a man with gold on his fingers and bright clothes walks into your synagogue" (James 2:2). Hermas's true prophet speaks in the church at prayer, not privately (43:8). It was also a plain Greek word for any assembly.

a: he takes pay for his prophecy
p: The surest sign of a false prophet: he will not prophesy without payment.
b: The Didache has the same test: "Whoever says in the Spirit, "Give me silver," or something else, you are not to listen to him" (Didache 11:12), and "it is by their ways that the false prophet and the prophet will be known" (Didache 11:8). Jesus' rule is "it is from their fruit that you will know them" (Matthew 7:20). Hermas adds the love of the 'seat of honor' (prōtokathedria, the Pharisees' 'best seats', Matthew 23:6) and a life of luxury.
r: Didache 11:8; Didache 11:12; Matthew 7:15-20; Matthew 23:6; Micah 3:11; 2 Peter 2:3

a: who says he carries the Spirit
p: Greek pneumatophoros: 'Spirit-bearing', a claim to inspiration.
b: Greek pneumatophoros, 'bearer of the Spirit'. In Hosea 9:7 the Greek (Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus) calls the prophet anthrōpos ho pneumatophoros, 'the Spirit-bearing man'. Hermas does not deny that there are true Spirit-bearers. He tells the church to test anyone who claims to be one by his works and life, as John says: "Put the spirits to the test, to find out if they come from God" (1 John 4:1).

a: makes a hole in the stone
p: Small things from above have great force: hail hurts, and drops wear through stone.
b: Job says, "water rubs stones smooth" (Job 14:19). Hermas's point is the source: what comes 'from above' has power, so the Spirit from God is strong, while the earthly spirit is like a stone thrown at the sky (43:18).

a: Remove every evil desire from yourself
p: Hermas sets a good desire against the evil one: desire is not evil in itself.
b: Greek epithymia, 'desire, craving', the word behind "You must not crave" (Romans 7:7). Paul usually uses it for evil desires (Galatians 5:16), but it can be good, as when Jesus longed to eat the Passover (Luke 22:15). Hermas calls evil desire wild and hard to tame (44:2) and tells the reader to 'rein it in', a horse's bridle, as James speaks of bridling the body and the tongue (James 3:2; James 1:26).

a: this evil desire is the devil's daughter
p: Double-mindedness and evil desire are both 'daughters of the devil'.
b: Hermas calls double-mindedness 'a daughter of the devil' (39:9) and evil desire the same (45:2). The picture makes vices into a family, as in 34:4 and 40:1, where grief is 'a sister' of double-mindedness and bad temper. Jesus told his opponents, "You come from your father, the devil" (John 8:44), the verse Clement of Alexandria quotes just before he quotes 43:3.

a: arm yourself with the fear of the Lord, and stand against them
p: The armor of God and James's 'stand up against the devil'.
b: Lake's margin points to Ephesians 6:13 ("pick up all of God's armor. Then you will be able to hold your ground on the evil day") and to James 4:7 ("Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you"). Hermas joins the two: armed with fear of the Lord, the believer stands, and desire runs away, as the devil does in 48:2.

a: Hand over to it the victory prize
p: Like an athlete, the winner hands his prize to the one he serves.
b: Hermas pictures the games: the victor is 'crowned' and brings his prize, Greek nikos, to the desire for righteousness, his new master. Paul uses athletes' crowns for the Christian life (1 Corinthians 9:25; 2 Timothy 4:8), and Revelation's elders lay their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10).

a: So he finished the twelve commandments
p: Some copies started the Parables here, not at 50.
b: Lake's note: 'There are some indications that in some recensions the Similitudes began here. A inserts ἀρχή before the next paragraph and E inserts initium similitudinum.' So the Athos manuscript writes 'beginning' at this point, and the Ethiopic version 'the beginning of the similitudes', though both go on with the dialogue about keeping the commandments. In Lake's text the Similitudes begin at 50.

a: I do not know if these commandments can be kept
p: Hermas fears the commandments are too hard; the Shepherd says belief makes them easy.
b: Moses had told Israel: "This command I am giving you today is not too strange or hard for you" (Deuteronomy 30:11), and John: "his commands are not heavy" (1 John 5:3). The Shepherd's answer in 46:5 sounds as if keeping them depends on one's own resolve, and his anger in 47:1 shows how seriously he means it. But 47:3 adds the key: the one who 'has the Lord in his heart' can master them, and 49:4 ends 'with the Lord making me strong'. Later Christians argued long over how human will and God's grace work together (Augustine against Pelagius); Hermas speaks to the practical despair of a sinner, not to that debate.

a: He created the world for humankind's sake
p: God made humankind ruler of creation, so they can rule the commandments too.
b: The Shepherd argues from Genesis 1:28, where God tells the man and woman to "Fill the earth and bring it under control", and from Psalm 8:6, "You set him as ruler over what your hands have made" (Lake's margin cites Psalm 8 by its Greek numbering). Lake's footnote reports that the Athos manuscript adds here a short prayer listing God's works (light and darkness, the earth, fruits, sun, moon, the stars' ordered motion, birds, beasts, reptiles and sea creatures) and ending with God making man master of them all; Lake calls it 'apparently a pious comment inserted in the text by mistake' and leaves it out.

a: those who have the Lord on their lips
p: Isaiah's complaint, quoted by Jesus: honor with the lips, a heart far away.
b: Jesus quotes Isaiah: "This people gives me honor with their lips, / but their heart keeps far away from me" (Matthew 15:8; Isaiah 29:13). Hermas uses the same pair, lips and a heart 'far from the Lord', and adds 'hardened', the word of 30:1.

a: The devil can wrestle with them, but he cannot throw them
p: Two wrestling words: the devil can grapple, but not pin.
b: Greek antipalaisai, 'wrestle against', and katapalaisai, 'wrestle down, throw'. Paul says, "For our wrestling match is not against blood and flesh" (Ephesians 6:12), with the related noun palē. Lake's margin at 48:2 points to James 4:7, the devil who runs away.

a: afraid that they have gone sour
p: A cellar owner checks only the partly empty jars, because they spoil.
b: Wine in a jar that was not full had air in it and soured into vinegar. A Roman cellar owner checking his stock would ignore the full jars and test the partly empty ones. So the devil 'tests' believers and finds his way only into the 'partly empty' (apokenos), those whose faith is not full. Compare the empty jar among full ones in 43:15.

a: as limp as a dead man's sinews
p: The devil's threat has no more strength than the tendons of a corpse.
b: Greek atonos ... hōsper nekrou neura, 'slack, like a dead man's sinews'. Atonos, 'without tension', picks up 47:7: 'his fear has no strength (tonos)'. The devil can threaten, but like a corpse's tendons, his threat cannot move.

a: fear the One who can do everything, save and destroy
t: The one who can save and destroy
p: James's title for God, the only Lawgiver and Judge.
b: Lake's margin points to James 4:12: "Only one is Lawgiver and Judge: the one who has power to save and to destroy." Jesus says to fear "the One who can destroy soul and body alike in Gehenna" (Matthew 10:28). Hermas sets this fear against the fear of the devil: fear God, and the devil cannot frighten you.

a: all the Lord's rulings
p: Greek dikaiōmata: God's righteous requirements.
b: Greek dikaiōmata, 'righteous requirements, rulings', the word behind 'rules' in Luke 1:6, where Zechariah and Elizabeth "walked in all the Lord's commands and rules". Hermas closes the Mandates with confidence and with dependence: 'with the Lord making me strong'.
